newsitem.title: USA: LDC capital flows to keep up post Fed-US investors.
newsitem.headline: LDC capital flows to keep up post Fed-US investors.

text.p: Capital flows to the emerging markets will likely persist after the Federal Reserve left U.S. rates steady, U.S. portfolio managers said on Tuesday.
Investment should continue even if the Fed does hike rates over the next few months, as is widely expected, because tightening comes at a gradual pace, investors said.

"Because the world has changed and tightening liquidity is more gradual than in the past, we will probably see the (emerging) markets holding their own," said Luis R. Luis, head of emerging market analysis at Scudder Stevens & Clark.

Luis said emerging debt prices would likely tighten around 100 basis points against comparable U.S. Treasuries by the end of the year, despite expectations the Fed would soon ratchet up interest rates again.
"The market is prepared to absorb a shift of 50 basis points in U.S. rates over the next six months," he said.

Anthony della Piana, portfolio manager at John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance, said that minor U.S. rate movements were probably irrelevant to the credit fundamentals of individual emerging market assets.

"A rapid rise in rates affecting market and global liquidity would be a concern, but from my perspective there is enough market liquidity that even a 1.0 percent move in rates, would not have a major impact," della Piana said.
The basis for healthy flows was improved credit conditions and the fact that Brady bonds still offered considerable yield advantage over comparable assets, investors said.
Luis added that higher U.S. rates might prompt some adjustments as players marginally shift toward emerging market fixed-income instruments and away from equities.
Not all investors shared the optimistic forecasts concerning the prospects foor emerging market assets.
Steve Merrell, senior portfolio manager at American Express Financial Services, said he expected short- to intermediate-term spread widening as an eventual Fed hike deprives the system of liquidity.

"When liquidity dries up and (investors) don't need a place to put so much of their money, there is going to be less of a demand for emerging market paper at a time when supply is increasing," Merrell said.
Merrell said he had shifted his portfolio to more defensive positions, emphasizing local currency instruments and shorter-maturity dollar paper.
